about.title: About us
about.paragraph1: P.U.L.S. is an educational physics platform that combines interactive simulations, problems and quizzes, theory resources across multiple chapters, and digital tools designed to make abstract ideas visible. We set out to go beyond a page of formulas: we want a place where you can practise for school or the baccalaureate, track your progress, and explore phenomena, from oscillations and waves to mechanics, thermodynamics, optics, and astronomy, in a modern, clear, and engaging way.
about.paragraph2: Our story began with a simple question: how can we make physical phenomena, especially oscillatory ones, come alive and become easier to understand? We are a team of students passionate about science, and we have always felt that beyond formulas and definitions there is a fascinating world full of rhythm, motion, and surprising links with nature and technology. From that starting point, P.U.L.S. grew into a broader platform: virtual simulations and experiments, collections of problems and baccalaureate-style papers, quick-practice quizzes, lessons grouped by topic, and profile tools with statistics so you can see your progress. Behind it all is the same curiosity: physics is not just symbols on a board, but motion, rhythm, and connections with the real world.

aboutPage.title: About us
aboutPage.description: P.U.L.S. is an educational physics platform that combines interactive simulations, problems and quizzes, theory resources across multiple chapters, and digital tools designed to make abstract ideas visible. We set out to go beyond a page of formulas: we want a place where you can practise for school or the baccalaureate, track your progress, and explore phenomena, from oscillations and waves to mechanics, thermodynamics, optics, and astronomy, in a modern, clear, and engaging way.
aboutPage.story1: Our story began with a simple question: how can we make physical phenomena, especially oscillatory ones, come alive and become easier to understand? We are a team of students passionate about science, and we have always felt that beyond formulas and definitions there is a fascinating world full of rhythm, motion, and surprising connections with nature and technology. From that starting point, P.U.L.S. grew into a broader platform: virtual simulations and experiments, collections of problems and baccalaureate-style papers, quick-practice quizzes, materials and lessons grouped by topic, plus profile tools with statistics so you can see your progress. Behind it all lies the same curiosity: physics is not just symbols on a board, but motion, rhythm, and links to the real world.
aboutPage.story2: We blended a passion for physics with modern web development and simulation tools (including environments such as Unity where the experience calls for advanced graphics and interaction) so that you can find both a browser-based laboratory and the matching exercises and resources in a single place. We have included both virtual experiments and recordings made in a real lab, wherever they aid understanding. We want anyone learning physics to find here not just an isolated simulation but a complete journey: from idea, to visualisation, to practice and review.
aboutPage.story3: It was not an easy road. We spent countless hours studying, coding, and testing every simulation, with the unconditional support of our mentor, Mrs. Ioana Bianka Bebu, and of our collaborator, the physicist Ion Bebu. We learned that, beyond numbers and equations, physics is a story about order and chaos, about how the universe dances to rhythms that are unseen yet perfectly regular.
aboutPage.story4: P.U.L.S. is not just a website but a window into a fascinating universe. It is proof that science can be beautiful, that it can inspire, and that through curiosity and hard work we can make complex things accessible and astonishing.
aboutPage.story5: So, if you want to see how the world moves to an unseen rhythm, we invite you to explore the platform. Discover, experiment, and let yourself be carried away by the fascinating PULS of science!

intro.subtitle: Properties of simple harmonic oscillation.
intro.p1: The harmonic linear oscillator is an idealised physical model that describes periodic motion of an object subjected to a restoring force proportional to its displacement from equilibrium. It is fundamental in mechanics, electromagnetism, acoustics — and appears even in quantum descriptions.
intro.p2: Try our simulations to see how harmonic oscillators behave and to build intuition about period, frequency and amplitude.

waves.title: Waves
waves.introLead: Waves transmit oscillations — mechanical, electromagnetic or other — between points in matter or vacuum.
waves.mechanicalParagraph: A mechanical wave is a local disturbance spreading through an elastic medium because neighbouring particles interact through elastic restoring forces — hence mechanical waves are also called elastic waves.
waves.electromagneticParagraph: Electromagnetic waves arise from perpendicular electric and magnetic fields that regenerate each another and travel together through space. Unlike mechanical waves they need no medium, so electromagnetic waves propagate also in vacuum.
waves.longitudinalParagraph: In longitudinal waves the particle motions are parallel to the propagation direction: the medium is alternately compressed and rarefied along the propagation path.
waves.transverseParagraph: In transverse waves the particle motions lie perpendicular to the propagation direction.

lissajous.title: Lissajous figures
lissajous.p1: Two oscillations combine to trace a graph called a Lissajous curve (often pronounced “Liss-uh-joo”). One oscillation drives the x coordinate and the other drives y. The curve shows how both motions evolve together in time.
lissajous.p2: When the frequency ratio is rational (expressible as a ratio of integers a/b), the curve closes and retraces the same loop. Different ratios give different shapes.
lissajous.p3: Lissajous figures are plane curves that describe motion obtained by combining two perpendicular sinusoidal oscillations with different frequencies and phases.
lissajous.p4: They are named after Jules Antoine Lissajous, who studied them in the 19th century.
lissajous.p5: They are plotted using parametric equations and appear on an oscilloscope when two electrical signals drive perpendicular axes.
lissajous.p6: They are commonly used to study frequency and phase relationships between two signals.
lissajous.examplesP: The shape depends on the frequency ratio and the phase difference between the two oscillations.

earthquakes.title: Earthquakes
earthquakes.p1: An earthquake is a sudden release of energy inside Earth that generates seismic waves.
earthquakes.p2: Earthquakes are caused by rapid stress release in the crust, producing seismic waves that propagate through the planet.
earthquakes.p3: These waves can be recorded by seismographs and are used to study Earth's interior structure.
earthquakes.p4: Our simulations provide a visual picture of how seismic waves propagate and interact with different materials.

earthquakes.c1: Seismic waves propagate through Earth's interior.
earthquakes.c2: There are several wave types (P, S, Love, Rayleigh, and more).
earthquakes.c3: Seismographs record ground motion from these waves.
earthquakes.c4: P-waves are longitudinal (compressional); S-waves are transverse (shear).
earthquakes.c5: Surface waves (e.g. Love and Rayleigh) often cause the strongest shaking and damage at the surface.
earthquakes.c6: P-waves travel faster than S-waves in the same material.
earthquakes.c7: S-waves do not propagate through the outer liquid core; P-waves do.

seo.title: Mechanics resources | Oscillations and collisions - PULS
seo.description: Mechanics: harmonic motion on horizontal and vertical axes, collisions, inclined plane, projectile motion, elastic chains and air drag — theory, formulas and simulations.
seo.keywords: mechanics, oscillations, collisions, inclined plane, projectile, elastic chain, air resistance, PULS

intro.p1: Mechanics studies how bodies move and the forces that cause motion. Here we focus on oscillatory motion and collisions — the foundation for understanding many more complex phenomena.
intro.p2: Oscillatory motion repeats periodically in time and appears in almost every physical system, from pendulums to atomic vibrations. Restoring forces tend to bring the system back toward equilibrium.
intro.p3: Collisions are processes in which two or more bodies interact through contact forces for a short time, exchanging momentum and kinetic energy according to conservation laws.

oscOX.title: Harmonic oscillation along the x-axis
oscOX.p1: Motion along OX describes horizontal oscillation of a body under a restoring force proportional to displacement. It is central to understanding oscillator response in time.
oscOX.p2: When the body is displaced from equilibrium on OX, the restoring force F = −kx (Hooke's law) pulls it back. This yields simple harmonic motion with explicit equations for position, velocity and acceleration.
oscOX.formulasHeading: Equations for harmonic oscillation along OX:

oscOY.title: Harmonic oscillation along the vertical axis (OY)
oscOY.p1: The vertical harmonic oscillator models a mass on a spring oscillating vertically — gravity and elastic force combine.
oscOY.p2: Equilibrium is no longer at x = 0; it shifts to where the spring force balances weight, depending on mass and spring constant.
oscOY.formulasHeading: Equations for harmonic oscillation along OY:
oscOY.variablesNote: where: y₀ is the equilibrium position, A the amplitude, ω the angular frequency, φ the initial phase, k the spring constant, m the mass and g gravitational acceleration.

collision.title: Collisions
collision.p1: Collisions are central in mechanics: two or more bodies interact through contact forces for a short time. They are essential for understanding momentum and energy conservation.
collision.p2: During a collision internal interaction forces dominate external ones, so conservation principles apply. Main types: elastic (kinetic energy conserved) and inelastic (part of kinetic energy converted to other forms).
collision.variablesNote: where: m₁, m₂ are masses, v₁ᵢ, v₂ᵢ initial speeds, v₁f, v₂f final speeds, e is the coefficient of restitution (e = 1 perfectly elastic, e = 0 perfectly inelastic).

inclined.title: Inclined plane
inclined.p1: The inclined plane is a classic setting for force analysis: weight splits into components that drive motion along the slope.
inclined.p2: It links force, acceleration and potential energy and is the basis for many mechanics and engineering problems.
inclined.variablesNote: where: m is mass, g gravitational acceleration, α slope angle, μ friction coefficient, h vertical height of the plane, N the normal force.

projectile.title: Projectile motion
projectile.p1: Projectile motion describes a body launched with initial speed in a uniform gravitational field (air resistance usually neglected). It combines uniform horizontal motion with uniformly accelerated vertical motion.
projectile.p2: The path is parabolic for given launch speed and angle. The simulator lets you vary angle, speed and launch height to see range, maximum height and time of flight.
projectile.variablesNote: where: v₀ is initial speed, α launch angle above the horizontal, g gravitational acceleration, y₀ initial height, T time of flight, R horizontal range.

elasticChains.title: Elastic chains
elasticChains.p1: An elastic chain consists of masses connected by Hookean springs. It models wave propagation in a discrete medium and collective motion of coupled oscillators.
elasticChains.p2: You can watch how a disturbance propagates along the chain, reflections at ends, and how energy is shared among masses — linking discrete models to continuous waves.

elasticChains.variablesNote: where: m is each mass, k the spring constant, and xᵢ the displacement of mass i from equilibrium. Neighbour differences produce forces that carry the disturbance along the chain.

airDrag.title: Air resistance (aerodynamic drag)
airDrag.p1: When a body moves through a fluid (air, water, …), the fluid exerts a drag force opposing motion. In the usual turbulent regime it grows roughly with the square of speed.
airDrag.p2: Shape, cross-sectional area and fluid density set how large the drag is — e.g. a flat sheet falls differently from the same paper crumpled into a ball. When drag balances weight, the body reaches terminal speed and stops accelerating.
airDrag.p3: Drag matters in aerospace, ballistics, sports and vehicle design. The Reynolds number tells whether flow is laminar or turbulent and strongly affects drag.

intro.p1: Electricity is the branch of physics that studies electric charge, currents, electric and magnetic fields and their interactions. It underpins modern technology.
intro.p2: It includes circuit analysis, Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws, electrical energy and power, and behaviour of resistors, capacitors and inductors.
intro.p3: Understanding electricity is essential for designing and analysing systems from simple circuits to large power networks.

circuits.title: Electric circuits
circuits.p1: Circuits are closed paths for current. Analysis rests on Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's rules.
circuits.p2: A circuit may contain resistors, voltage sources, capacitors, inductors — each affecting overall behaviour.
circuits.variablesNote: where: U voltage, I current, R resistance, P power, W energy, q charge, t time, ρ resistivity, l conductor length, S cross-sectional area, n charge carrier density, v drift speed.

kirchhoff.title: Kirchhoff's laws
kirchhoff.p1: For multi-node, multi-loop circuits Ohm's law alone is not enough. Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) expresses charge conservation at each node; Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL) expresses energy conservation around each closed loop.
kirchhoff.p2: The simulator below lets you build and analyse such circuits interactively.

energy.title: Energy in circuits
energy.p1: Electrical energy is associated with charge motion in a circuit. It can be converted to heat, light, mechanical work, etc.
energy.p2: Energy balance is crucial for efficiency and consumption. Energy supplied by sources equals energy absorbed by components (conservation).
energy.variablesNote: where: W energy, P power, C capacitance, L inductance, Q charge, η efficiency.

seo.keywords: thermodynamics, entropy, Carnot, heat engine, ideal gas, periodic table, PULS

intro.p1: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that studies energy transformations and the laws governing them. It describes macroscopic systems using thermodynamic variables such as temperature, pressure, volume and internal energy.
intro.p2: Core ideas include internal energy, entropy, heat, work and thermodynamic potentials. They are linked by the fundamental laws that govern physical and chemical processes.
intro.p3: Thermodynamics is essential for heat engines, refrigeration, chemical processes and many natural and technological phenomena involving energy transfer and conversion.

fundamental.title: Fundamental thermodynamic processes
fundamental.p1: Thermodynamics studies energy transformations and the laws governing them. Key concepts are temperature, pressure, volume, internal energy and entropy.
fundamental.p2: A thermodynamic system is described by state variables such as pressure (p), volume (V), temperature (T) and particle number (N). They are related by equations of state that describe each substance.
fundamental.p3: Processes may be reversible or irreversible, isothermal, isobaric, isochoric or adiabatic — each with specific equations reflecting energy conservation and entropy increase.
fundamental.variablesNote: where: U internal energy, Q heat, L work, p pressure, V volume, n moles, R gas constant, T temperature, S entropy, k_B Boltzmann constant, Ω number of microstates, f degrees of freedom, H enthalpy, F Helmholtz free energy, G Gibbs free energy, κ isothermal compressibility, α thermal expansion coefficient, η efficiency, T_C cold reservoir temperature, T_H hot reservoir temperature.

engines.title: Heat engines
engines.p1: Heat engines convert thermal energy (heat) from a hot reservoir into useful mechanical work, rejecting part of the energy to a cold reservoir. Examples include internal combustion engines (Otto, Diesel), gas and steam turbines, and the idealised Carnot engine.
engines.p2: The heat-engine simulator lets you visualise thermodynamic cycles on p–V and T–s diagrams, compare efficiencies and understand each phase: compression, heating/combustion, expansion and exhaust.
engines.variablesNote: where: η is efficiency, L_{util} useful mechanical work per cycle, Q_H heat absorbed from the hot reservoir, Q_C heat rejected to the cold reservoir, T_H and T_C absolute temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs; the contour integral \(\oint p\,dV\) is the p–V cycle area (net work per cycle).

combustionEngines.title: Internal combustion engines
combustionEngines.p1: Internal combustion engines convert the energy released when fuel burns into mechanical work through piston motion. The best-known types are four-stroke engines (Otto petrol and Diesel) and two-stroke engines.
combustionEngines.p2: The animated simulator shows the four phases — intake, compression, power/expansion and exhaust — on a 4-stroke engine, compares petrol, diesel and 2-stroke cycles, and links piston motion to the p–V diagram: the enclosed area is the mechanical work produced in one complete cycle.

periodicTable.title: Periodic table (useful quantities for problems)
periodicTable.p1: The periodic table gives element symbols, atomic number Z and — especially — molar mass M for mole, particle and concentration calculations. These quantities appear often in gases, mixtures, calorimetry and the ideal gas law.
periodicTable.variablesNote: where: Z proton count, A mass number, N neutron count, n amount of substance (moles), m mass, M molar mass, N_A Avogadro constant, c molar concentration, V volume.

seo.title: Optics resources | Lenses, reflection and refraction - PULS

seo.keywords: optics, lenses, reflection, refraction, Snell, prism, laser, electromagnetic spectrum, PULS

intro.p1: Optics studies light: its behaviour and properties and its interaction with matter. It spans geometrical optics, physical optics and quantum optics.
intro.p2: Topics include reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarisation — essential for optical systems from simple lenses to complex instruments.
intro.p3: Applications range from lighting and medical imaging to lasers and optical fibre.

thinLens.title: Thin lenses
thinLens.p1: Thin lenses refract light to form images. They may be converging (convex) or diverging (concave), each with characteristic image formation.
thinLens.p2: Thin-lens equations relate object and image distances and sizes — the basis of many optical systems.
thinLens.variablesNote: where: f focal length, x₁ object distance, x₂ image distance, β linear magnification, y₁ object height, y₂ image height, C optical power (convergence), n refractive index, R₁ and R₂ radii of curvature, γ angular magnification, α₁ and α₂ angles.

refractionReflection.title: Refraction and reflection
refractionReflection.p1: Refraction and reflection describe light at interfaces between media with different refractive indices. They follow the laws of reflection and refraction.
refractionReflection.p2: Snell's law relates incidence and refraction angles to the indices. Total internal reflection occurs when light goes from a higher to a lower index. Many effects — desert mirages or objects appearing bent in water — come from how the index varies.
refractionReflection.variablesNote: where: n refractive index, c speed of light in vacuum, v speed in medium, i and r incidence and refraction angles, θ₁ and θ₂ angles in the two media, θᵢ and θᵣ incidence and reflection angles, θcrit critical angle, λ₀ wavelength in vacuum, λₙ wavelength in medium.

prism.title: Prism and dispersion of light
prism.p1: A prism refracts light and splits it into spectral components. Dispersion occurs because the refractive index depends on wavelength.
prism.p2: Dispersion explains rainbows and underpins many optical instruments. Studying prisms clarifies light behaviour in dispersive media.
prism.variablesNote: where: δ deviation angle, A apex angle of the prism, i₁ and i₂ incidence and emergence angles, D angular dispersion with respect to λ, P dispersive power, n_F, n_C, n_D refractive indices at standard spectral lines, A,B,C Cauchy coefficients (not the apex).

atmospheric.title: Atmospheric refraction
atmospheric.p1: Atmospheric refraction bends light through layers of different density. It causes mirages and lets the Sun appear above the horizon when it is already geometrically below it.
atmospheric.p2: It matters for astronomy, navigation and meteorology and shows how atmospheric optical properties affect observations.
atmospheric.variablesNote: where: n_air air refractive index, T temperature (K), p pressure (hPa), e water vapour pressure, θᵢ incidence angle, θᵣ refraction angle, Δθ refraction correction, z zenith distance.

laser.title: Laser
laser.p1: A laser produces a coherent, nearly monochromatic beam with low divergence. In applications (telecom, medicine, metrology), wavelength, frequency, energy and intensity are linked.

intro.p1: We introduce two core phenomena: amplitude superposition in the double-slit experiment (interference and probability) and penetration of a potential barrier (tunnelling). Below each simulation are commonly used formulas with short explanations.

doubleSlit.title: Double-slit experiment
doubleSlit.p1: A beam passes through two parallel slits. In the quantum description the amplitude on the screen is the sum of contributions from each slit; measured intensity follows Born's rule and can show interference fringes. If you localize the particle on one path before the screen, the pattern changes — wave–particle complementarity.

doubleSlit.fringeLead: On a screen at distance L ≫ d from the slits, in the small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ y/L, the spacing between consecutive maxima of order m and m+1 on the screen is approximately:
doubleSlit.fringeNote: The closer the slits (small d) or the longer the wavelength, the farther apart the fringes on the screen.
doubleSlit.bornLead: The probability of detecting the particle in a small region of space is proportional to the squared modulus of the wavefunction (the sum of amplitudes for all relevant paths):
doubleSlit.bornNote: That is why interference is seen: terms that add in ψ can produce maxima or minima of |ψ|², not merely a sum of independent intensities.

tunnelling.title: Quantum tunnelling
tunnelling.p1: In regions where classically the kinetic energy would be negative (E < V(x)), the wavefunction does not vanish abruptly: inside the barrier an evanescent part appears that decays exponentially, so there is non-zero probability of finding the particle beyond the barrier — tunnelling. It occurs in tunnel diodes, scanning tunnelling microscopes (STM) and many nuclear and chemical models.

tunnelling.schroNote: In each region where V is approximately constant, the solution is a combination of exponentials (oscillatory if E > V, growing/decaying if E < V).

tunnelling.kappaNote: The higher the barrier relative to E (i.e. the larger V₀ − E), the larger κ and the faster the wave decays inside the barrier.

tunnelling.transNote: Exact numerical factors depend on the barrier shape (step, smooth, etc.), but the exponential dependence on κ a explains why tunnelling is sensitive to a few ångströms in STM or layer thickness in real devices.

tunnelling.heisenbergNote: Useful when estimating level widths or lifetimes in processes involving tunnelling from a confined state.

bonding.title: Bonding between atoms and molecular orbitals
bonding.p1: Beyond the isolated atom, quantum mechanics explains why atoms can bind into stable molecules: linear combinations of atomic orbitals lead to bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals. Increased probability density between nuclei corresponds to a lower total energy than separated atoms.

bonding.moNote: In the bonding orbital, the probability density |ψ_bond|² is larger between the nuclei, lowering the total energy compared to separated atoms.

bonding.ebindNote: The larger E_bind, the stronger the bond and the more stable the molecule.

bonding.forceNote: The effective constant k relates to bond “stiffness”; vibrational frequency depends on k and the reduced mass of the two atoms.

bonding.rhoNote: High density between nuclei is the hallmark of a covalent bond; in the antibonding orbital this density is small or zero between nuclei.

seo.title: Lasers | ELI-NP and interactive simulators - PULS
seo.description: Lasers: core ideas, useful formulas, modern applications, ELI‑NP context, and interactive simulators on laser–matter interaction, high-intensity pulses, and laser wakefield acceleration.
seo.keywords: lasers, laser, ELI-NP, Măgurele, laser optics, laser intensity, Gaussian beam, femtosecond pulse

lasers.pageTitle: Lasers: from photons to extreme pulses

intro.p1: A laser is a light source with high coherence, very good directionality and, in many applications, a well-controlled wavelength. That combination makes it useful both in laboratory optics and in medicine, telecommunications, metrology or plasma physics.
intro.p2: At Măgurele, the ELI‑NP facility is a European reference for high-power laser experiments, where laser–matter interaction opens discussion of plasma, particle acceleration and extreme conditions in an educationally inspired, real-research setting.

about.title: Lasers in brief
about.p1: A laser produces coherent, directional light that is easy to focus. That makes it ideal for precise measurements, telecommunications, medicine and experiments where energy must be concentrated in a very small region.
about.p2: When using a laser simulator, pay special attention to wavelength, power, spot diameter and pulse duration — these set intensity, ionisation and the physical regime of interaction with matter.

eliHistory.title: Short ELI‑NP history
eliHistory.p1: ELI‑NP, developed at Măgurele, is part of the European Extreme Light Infrastructure and was conceived for research at the intersection of high-power lasers and nuclear physics.
eliHistory.p2: For students, ELI‑NP matters because it shows how seemingly theoretical ideas — focusing, peak power or laser–matter interaction — become central in frontier experiments.

sim1.title: Simulator 1: Laser vs matter
sim1.intro: This simulator explores how the beam interacts with the target: by changing interaction mode, material and beam parameters you can observe heating, photoemission or ionisation.
sim1.factsHeading: What to notice in the simulator

intensity.title: Beam intensity
intensity.explanation: If the spot area shrinks, intensity rises rapidly. In the simulator this immediately affects the material response.

photon.title: Photon energy
photon.explanation: Wavelength controls each photon's energy and thus the likelihood of processes such as the photoelectric effect.

radiationPressure.title: Radiation pressure
radiationPressure.explanation: Light carries momentum; at high intensities it can transfer measurable pressure to an illuminated surface.

facts.f2: materials respond differently to heating and ionisation
facts.f3: interaction modes help compare thermal effects with photoelectric ones

peakPower.title: Peak pulse power
peakPower.explanation: When pulse energy is compressed into an extremely short duration, instantaneous power becomes very large.

peakIntensity.title: Peak intensity
peakIntensity.explanation: High power combined with good focusing leads to extreme regimes where plasma and ablation appear.

gaussianDiv.title: Gaussian beam divergence
gaussianDiv.explanation: A very tightly focused beam usually diverges more after the focal region.

rayleigh.title: Rayleigh range
rayleigh.explanation: This distance indicates the region around the focus where the beam stays relatively collimated.

facts.f1: ELI‑NP is linked to extreme laser research at Măgurele

sim3.title: Simulator 3: Laser wakefield accelerator

intensity.title: Beam intensity

relEnergy.title: Relativistic energy

facts.f1: higher intensity increases wakefield amplitude and electron acceleration
facts.f2: plasma density changes the wave period and capture conditions
facts.f3: if the electron falls out of the accelerating phase, energy gain drops

hydrogen.title: Hydrogen atom
hydrogen.p1: The hydrogen atom is the simplest: one proton and one electron. It was an ideal “laboratory” for developing quantum mechanics because its emission spectrum has very clear, sharp lines.
hydrogen.bohrP1: Niels Bohr (1913) proposed that the electron cannot have arbitrary energy, only discrete values (energy levels). For hydrogen, the energy of quantum level n = 1, 2, 3, … is:
hydrogen.bohrP2: The value 13.6 eV is the ionisation energy of hydrogen (energy needed to remove the electron from the ground level n = 1 to infinity). The minus sign shows the electron is bound to the proton.
hydrogen.transP1: When the electron jumps from a higher level E_m to a lower one E_n, the energy difference is emitted as a photon:
hydrogen.transP2: The wavelengths of hydrogen spectral lines follow the Rydberg formula:
hydrogen.transP3: where R_H is the Rydberg constant for hydrogen; spectral series (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, …) correspond to different values of n.
hydrogen.waveP1: In modern quantum mechanics, the electron in hydrogen is described by a wavefunction ψ_{nℓm}(r,θ,φ) that satisfies the Schrödinger equation in the Coulomb potential of the proton:
hydrogen.waveP2: The solutions yield the same energy levels E_n as Bohr's model, but also orbital shapes (s, p, d, …) and probabilities for finding the electron around the nucleus.

periodicTable.title: The periodic table of elements
periodicTable.p1: Elements are arranged by atomic number Z. Within a group, atoms have similar outer-shell configurations; across a period, both protons in the nucleus and electrons in shells increase.

electromagnetism.pageTitle: Electromagnetism: fields, forces and modern applications

intro.p1: Electromagnetism describes how electric charge, electric field, magnetic field and electromagnetic waves are linked. It is a pillar of modern physics and the basis of today's electrical technology.
intro.p2: Here you find superconductivity (Meissner effect, levitation) and a PEM fuel cell: how H₂ and O₂ produce current through charge separation and electron flow in the external circuit.

meissner.title: Superconductivity and the Meissner effect
meissner.intro: Here you can see electromagnetism directly: magnetic field, levitation and transition to the normal state when temperature exceeds T_c.

tc.title: Superconductivity condition
tc.explanation: Below the critical temperature T_c the material becomes superconducting and magnetic field screening appears.

fm.title: Magnetic force (educational model)
fm.explanation: In the simulator the repulsive effect grows with the square of magnetic field B and decreases as distance h increases.

balance.title: Vertical balance
balance.explanation: Stable levitation occurs when magnetic force balances weight (F_m ≈ mg).

london.title: London penetration depth
london.explanation: Describes the scale over which the magnetic field penetrates the superconductor before being screened.

fuelCell.title: PEM fuel cell
fuelCell.intro: A proton-exchange membrane cell converts the chemical energy of hydrogen and oxygen into electric current: at the anode H₂ is oxidised, electrons travel through the external circuit, and H⁺ crosses the membrane to the cathode where O₂ is reduced and water forms.

global.title: Overall reaction (educative model)
global.explanation: Chemical balance of the hydrogen cell: hydrogen and oxygen are consumed, water is produced, and part of the released energy appears as electrical work in the circuit.

power.title: Electrical power delivered to the load
power.explanation: Useful power at the terminals is the product of voltage U and current I. In the simulator, higher flows or lower bulb resistance increase I and thus P.

ohm.title: Ohm's law (simple load)
ohm.explanation: For a resistive load R, current is tied to available voltage. The teaching model also limits current by reactant flow.

efficiency.title: Efficiency (working definition)
efficiency.explanation: Efficiency compares electrical power output to power available from the chemical flow of reactants. H₂/O₂ imbalance or internal losses reduce η.

intro.p1: Mathematics supplies the precise language used to describe physical phenomena. Here we explore graphing functions and visualizing geometric objects in four-dimensional space — useful in analysis and theoretical physics alike.
intro.p2: Function plots reveal relationships between quantities, while the 4D visualizer shows how geometric objects extend into higher dimensions.

graphs.title: Function graphs
graphs.p: Graphs highlight domains, codomains, zeros, extrema and limiting behaviour. Elementary functions — polynomial, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic — are foundational in physics modelling.

fourD.title: 4D visualizer
fourD.p: Four-dimensional space extends ideas from 3D geometry. We cannot "see" the fourth dimension directly, but we can project 4D objects (such as the hypercube) into 3D or 2D, just as we project a cube onto a sheet. These ideas appear in relativity (spacetime) and advanced mathematics.

fourD.p_proj: You obtain a 3D 'shadow' of a 4D object, analogous to projecting a cube onto a plane yielding a hexagon or square.

fourD.p_minkowski: In relativity the fourth dimension is time; the Minkowski metric describes distances in spacetime.

seo.title: Astronomy | Constellations, Kepler, planetary motion, Michelson–Morley - PULS
seo.description: Constellations and sky coordinates, Kepler's laws, planetary motion and the Michelson–Morley experiment: lesson materials, formulas and simulations.
seo.keywords: astronomy, constellations, Kepler's laws, Michelson-Morley, orbits, planetary motion, stars, PULS

intro.p1: Below we begin with the night sky: how groups of stars are named (constellations), how you can navigate, and how astronomers specify a star's position on the celestial sphere. We then move to planetary motion: in the early 17th century Johannes Kepler formulated three laws for elliptical orbits around the Sun; today we connect them with Newtonian gravity and, for fine detail, general relativity.
intro.p2: Finally, the Michelson–Morley experiment explains why the speed of light in vacuum does not depend on an "ether wind" — a key step toward special relativity, relevant to astronomical interferometry.

constellations.title: Constellations
constellations.p1: Constellations are regions and stellar patterns recognised across many cultures; modern astronomy recognises 88 official constellations. On charts, stellar positions use right ascension alpha (like longitude on the celestial equator, in hours, minutes, seconds) and declination delta (angle from the celestial equator, like latitude). The simulator lets you explore the sky, brief legends and practical orientation hints (e.g. toward Polaris).
constellations.p2: Important: the tropical zodiac used in horoscopes does not match astronomers' constellations; Earth's axis and orbit slowly drift against the stellar background. The simulation shows an astronomical sky map, not astrological forecasts.

kepler.title: Kepler's three laws
kepler.p: The simulation shows the elliptical orbit, the Sun at a focus, how planetary speed varies, and how orbital period relates to the semi-major axis.
kepler.law1P: Planets move on elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus. The semi-major axis is a and eccentricity e measures how 'flattened' the ellipse is.
kepler.law2P: The radius vector (Sun–planet line) sweeps equal areas in equal times. The planet moves fastest near perihelion and slowest near aphelion.

kepler.law3Title: Law III — Period and semi-major axis
kepler.law3P: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. The ratio T squared / a cubed is the same for all planets orbiting the Sun.
kepler.law3Note: Where: T is period, a semi-major axis, G gravitational constant, M Solar mass.

planetary.p: The planetary motion simulator visualises planetary orbits in the solar system and how they arise from attraction toward the central star. For tightly bound orbits, general-relativity corrections explain effects such as Mercury's perihelion precession.

planetary.grNote: This expression (radians per orbit) shows how much the ellipse's major axis rotates each revolution in general relativity. The effect is tiny for ordinary planets but measurable for Mercury and is a classical test of Einstein's theory.

michelson.title: Michelson–Morley experiment
michelson.p1: In the late 19th century light was assumed to propagate through an invisible medium called "luminiferous ether". If so, Earth's motion through the ether ought to produce an "ether wind" changing the apparent speed of light along different directions.
michelson.p2: Albert A. Michelson and Edward W. Morley's experiment (1887) compared travel times along two perpendicular paths in an interferometer. The expected asymmetry did not appear: the speed of light seemed the same in all directions — paving the way for special relativity (Einstein, 1905), with implications for astronomical observations relying on interference.
michelson.p3: The interferometer splits a beam into two perpendicular arms of length L, reflects from mirrors and recombines the beams. Had an ether wind of speed v existed, travel times would differ slightly; in reality, within experimental precision the difference was zero — no privileged ether.

seo.title: Nuclear physics | U isotopes, U-235 fission, heavy water, D–T fusion - PULS
seo.description: Resources: uranium isotopes (nucleus model, alpha decay, chart of all 26 isotopes), chain fission (U-235, multiplication factor k), D₂O vs H₂O, isotope exchange and fractional distillation plus an educational D–T fusion model (~17.6 MeV), with interactive simulators.
seo.keywords: nuclear physics, uranium isotopes, nuclide chart, alpha decay, fission, U-235, k factor, heavy water, D2O, fusion, deuterium, tritium, reactor, isotope exchange, moderator

intro.p1: This page brings together materials on induced fission in U-235, an educational D–T fusion model, heavy water and deuterium separation (isotope exchange, distillation), and—at the end—two uranium-isotope simulations (four key isotopes and the chart of all 26). The simulators are not substitutes for nuclear engineering curricula or safety analysis; they support intuition and high-school curricula.
intro.p2: Below: chain fission (U-235), D–T fusion, D₂O vs H₂O, isotope exchange and fractional distillation; lastly, uranium isotopes (four essentials plus the chart of 26).

fissionSim.title: Simulator: Nuclear chain fission (U-235)
fissionSim.p1: A thermal neutron can be captured by a U-235 nucleus (²³⁵₉₂U); the compound nucleus breaks into fission fragments, fresh neutrons (on average 2–3 per fission for U-235) and gamma rays. When each generation yields more than one neutron usable for further fissions, the effective multiplication factor exceeds 1 and power rises—the idea behind controlled chain reactions with rods and moderator.
fissionSim.p2: In the simulator each fission adds roughly 200 MeV to the cumulative energy (a pedagogical benchmark for energy per event). The displayed factor k is an empirical ratio between fission rates on successive time segments so you can discuss subcritical / critical / supercritical without claiming a complete reactor model.
fissionSim.alt: U-235 chain fission simulator: neutrons, nuclei, k factor and cumulative energy
fissionSim.formulasTitle: Formulas tied to the simulator model
fissionSim.h_induced_p: Neutron capture and fragments (nu = number of emitted neutrons; masses and Z depend on the fission channel):
fissionSim.h_induced_note: Conservation requires 235 + 1 = A₁ + A₂ + nu and 92 = Z₁ + Z₂.
fissionSim.h_etot_p: Let N count fissions and averaged E mean energy released per fission (200 MeV in the app):
fissionSim.h_qmass_p: Typical order of magnitude: Q of tens of MeV per emitted nucleon; total per fission on the hundreds of MeV—that is why the teaching model rounds to ~200 MeV.
fissionSim.h_k_p: In a generation picture the multiplication factor is written as the ratio of useful neutrons between successive generations. The app estimates an empirical k from the evolution of the fission rate, not microscopic cross sections:
fissionSim.h_k_tail: k < 1 subcritical; k ~= 1 critical (on average stable); k > 1 supercritical—power rises unless cooling/absorption intervene (SCRAM rods in simulation).

fusionSim.title: Simulator: D–T fusion reactor
fusionSim.p1: Each fusion event near the nucleus in the simulator adds 17.6 MeV—the standard textbook value for a deuterium plus tritium reaction. Controls (temperature, pressure, neutron flux) tune particle speeds, overlap probability near the nucleus and stability; beyond a critical threshold the demonstration switches into a purely illustrative meltdown scenario.
fusionSim.p2: Parameters in the UI: temperature (0–1000 K), pressure (0–100 relative scale), neutron flux (0–10). The fusion zone widens mildly with cumulative energy; meltdown triggers when flux exceeds ~8.5 while temperature exceeds ~850 K simultaneously.

fusionSim.h_q_dt_note: Q ~ 17.6 MeV for D–T is the simulator benchmark per event; in a real reactor energy is shared among particles and structure—confinement and materials are not modelled.
fusionSim.h_stab_p: The app shows qualitative states such as OK / unstable before meltdown; triggering is effectively large flux AND large temperature simultaneously. There is no single universal physics formula—just a pedagogical threshold for discussing power feedback and cooling.

historyRo.title: Brief history and Romanian context
historyRo.p1: In Romania debates about heavy water tie into nuclear infrastructure and the era when national facilities separated deuterium isotopes. Physicist Dorel Mihai Constantinescu is associated with process modelling relevant to manufacturing D₂O.
historyRo.p2: In the 1970s at Plant G in Râmnicu Vâlcea he worked on computing and simulation of processes aimed at obtaining heavy water, bridging from design concepts to tangible experimental milestones.
historyRo.p3: For students this link helps show that heavy water is not only formulae—it belongs to Romanian nuclear-engineering history, to the moderator role in reactors, and to how research, engineering and simulation worked together.

heavyWater.title: What the heavy-water simulator compares (D₂O vs H₂O)
heavyWater.p: Code-wise the Body section uses an educational slider for a fictitious molar fraction of D₂O with a coloured status ladder (explicitly labelled as educational only). Physics compares indicative properties (boiling point, density, frequency), while Reactor sketches schematic neutron-capture contrasts for D₂O versus H₂O.

heavyWater.h_frac_p: For a mixture modelled by the simulator, the D₂O percentage is:
heavyWater.h_frac_note: The fraction is illustrative for intuition; not a clinical instrument nor a direct depiction of physiological concentration.
heavyWater.h_freq_p: Harmonic oscillator style: frequency scales inversely with the square root of reduced mass:
heavyWater.h_freq_note: The simulator reduced-mass-ratio slider embodies heavier D₂O giving lower characteristic frequencies.

exchange.title: Isotope-exchange plant (H₂S–H₂O)
exchange.p1: This simulator sketches how isotope-exchange enriches deuterium in water. Beyond the textbook formula alone you witness stage-wise effects, mass transfer and overall efficiency tendencies.
exchange.p2: The model is educational—meant for main trends of isotopic separation rather than sizing a real industrial unit.
exchange.p3: In Romanian technological history Constantinescu detailed why separating heavy water is hard: chemistry of H₂O and D₂O is nearly alike, useful distinctions are mostly physical, while raising enrichment from roughly 140 ppm natural abundance to reactor-grade ~99.8% demands sprawling plant and enormous energy expenditure.
exchange.h_alpha_note: The factor alpha shows how efficiently isotopes divide between phases at equilibrium. Larger alpha means more enrichment per ideal stage.
exchange.h_mass_note: Relates feed flow F at concentration x_F to product P and waste W streams.
exchange.h_stage_note: Higher useful stage count n boosts deuterium concentration when each stage contributes net separation.
exchange.h_twostep_p: Industrial descriptions for Plant G emphasise primary enrichment (large flow, modest concentration, dominates energy demand) versus finishing flows (tiny throughput pushing up to ~99.8% D₂O).
exchange.h_twostep_p2: The canonical scheme chains H₂O–H₂S isotope-exchange in thermal columns (cold + hot towers) with vacuum distillation / rectification for the final polishing step—the simulator conveys cascade logic and optimisation of liquid-to-gas ratio.

distillation.title: Fractional distillation: from ~20% to reactor-grade heavy water
distillation.p1: After isotope-exchange drives concentrations toward tens-of-percent regimes, polishing relies on the small boiling gap between H₂O and D₂O (~1.4 °C): a rectification tower with many stages, vigorous reflux and a bottom reboiler concentrates D₂O at the column bottom while vapour leaning toward H₂O rises toward the condenser.
distillation.p2: The schematic tracks purity versus time alongside reflux influence and theoretical stages—emphasising why the last fractions toward ~99.8% are the costliest; the fractional-distillation simulator stays locked until the exchange simulation finishes (saved locally).
distillation.alt: H₂O–D₂O fractional distillation simulator: column, reflux and purity plot
distillation.h_vol_p: Let L denote the more volatile fraction (H₂O) and H the less volatile (D₂O); at equilibrium:
distillation.h_vol_note: For H₂O/D₂O, relative volatility is close to simulator default ~1.06, so each stage barely separates—that many stages plus high reflux.
distillation.h_eq_p: With liquid and vapour mole fractions x, y for H₂O and constant pedagogical alpha:
distillation.h_eq_note: Liquid D₂O mole fraction equals 1 − x; at the column bottom rectification lowers x raising D₂O fraction.
distillation.h_R_note: L is reflux molar flow returning downward, D the overhead draw-off. Larger R improves separation but trims light-product throughput and lengthens timelines toward ultrahigh bottoms purity.
distillation.h_fenske_p: Didactic estimate of stages needed under total reflux between distillate mole fraction x_D and bottoms fraction x_B of the light species:
distillation.h_fenske_note: Real reflux ratios and efficiencies raise the actual stage count versus N_min; nonetheless alpha barely above 1 yields huge N for strong separation.
distillation.h_bp_p: Distillation exploitation rests on differing boiling temperatures; Delta T_b = T_b(D₂O) - T_b(H₂O) (~1.4 °C) implies relative volatility exceedingly close to 1.

uFour.title: Simulator: Uranium isotopes (nucleus, alpha, fission, time)
uFour.p: Uranium always has Z = 92 protons; isotopes differ by neutron count N hence mass number A = Z + N. The simulator spotlights four isotopes common in curricula (233…238 U): nucleus sketch, alpha decay (emission of ⁴₂He), a fission example on U‑235 plus a radioactive time machine using half-life-driven decay.

uFour.h_alpha_note: In this simulation alpha emission reduces daughter Z by two nucleons lost by four from the parent.

u26.title: Simulator: Chart of uranium’s 26 isotopes
u26.p: Experimentally 26 uranium isotopes are catalogued (mass numbers A spanning roughly 217–242). In nature prominent abundances boil down to U-234, U-235 and U-238; others arise in reactors or fleeting decay chains. The simulator colours dominant decay modes (alpha, beta minus, electron capture / beta plus), shows details upon selection, and overlays N(t) with lambda inferred from listed half-life.

u26.formulas_follow: Cell brightness conveys relative stability; educational figures aggregate public summaries rather than authoritative nuclear evaluations.

instalatie-schimb-izotopic.title: Isotope Exchange Plant (H2S-H2O)
instalatie-schimb-izotopic.description: Simulate the heavy-water separation process: stages, isotope exchange, concentration evolution, and process efficiency.
instalatie-schimb-izotopic.caption: Isotope exchange plant

distilare-d2o-fractionata.title: Fractional D2O Distillation
distilare-d2o-fractionata.description: Single column with reboiler and condenser: reflux, theoretical stages, low relative volatility, and the purity-versus-time curve following isotope exchange.
distilare-d2o-fractionata.caption: Fractional heavy-water distillation

frecare-aer.title: Air Resistance
frecare-aer.description: Compare the fall of two bodies in gravity with aerodynamic drag: terminal velocity, mass, shape, and cross-sectional area.
frecare-aer.caption: Air resistance in free fall

reactor-fuziune-dt.title: D-T Fusion Reactor (Educational Model)
reactor-fuziune-dt.description: Educational toy model for D–T fusion: temperature, pressure, and neutron flux change particle motion and fusion rate; cumulative energy (~17.6 MeV per event), stability warnings, time-series chart, and a visual meltdown scenario.
reactor-fuziune-dt.caption: Deuterium-tritium fusion model

fisiune-nucleara.title: Nuclear Chain Fission (U-235)
fisiune-nucleara.description: Neutron-induced fission in U-235, the release of 2-3 new neutrons, roughly 200 MeV per event, the multiplication factor k, and control rods in an educational visual model.
fisiune-nucleara.caption: Chain reaction and multiplication factor k

izotopi-uraniu.title: Uranium Isotopes: Nucleus, Alpha Decay, Fission, and Time
izotopi-uraniu.description: Four key uranium isotopes from U-233 to U-238: nuclear model, alpha decay, U-235 fission scenario, and a time machine using N(t) based on half-life.
izotopi-uraniu.caption: Uranium isotopes: nuclei and decay

toti-izotopii.title: Map of the 26 Uranium Isotopes
toti-izotopii.description: The Z = 92 line on the nuclide chart: all known isotopes from A = 217 to 242, decay modes, historical timeline, and the radioactive law N(t) with lambda and half-life.
toti-izotopii.caption: Uranium isotope map

criogenie.title: Cryogenics and States of Matter
criogenie.description: Explore low-temperature regimes: the pV = nRT relation, particle dynamics, and transitions between gas, liquid, and solid for different materials.
criogenie.caption: Cryogenics simulator

supraconductivitate.title: Superconductivity and the Meissner Effect
supraconductivitate.description: Simulate the T < Tc condition, magnetic levitation, and the transition back to the normal state when the temperature exceeds the critical temperature.
supraconductivitate.caption: Superconductivity

fuel-cell.title: PEM Fuel Cell
fuel-cell.description: Educational simulation: H2 and O2 feed the cell, electrons travel through the external circuit, protons cross the membrane, and voltage, current, power, and efficiency vary with flow rate and load.
fuel-cell.caption: PEM fuel cell
